title: Understanding IPO Taxation in India: STCG, LTCG & ITR Guide
description: Gains from selling IPO shares are taxed as capital gains once the shares are listed on the stock exchange. Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG) apply if listed sha.

faq.a: Yes, any profit made from selling IPO shares after they are listed is considered a capital gain and is subject to income tax in India.

faq.q: What is the holding period for IPO shares to determine STCG vs. LTCG?
faq.a: For listed equity shares, including IPO shares, if held for 12 months or less, gains are STCG. If held for more than 12 months, gains are LTCG.

faq.q: Can I offset losses from IPO investments against gains?
faq.a: Yes, capital losses can be set off against capital gains. Short-term capital losses (STCL) can be set off against both STCG and LTCG. Long-term capital losses (LTCL) can only be set off against LTCG. Unadjusted losses can be carried forward for up to eight assessment years.

faq.q: Do Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) have different IPO tax rules?
faq.a: Yes, NRIs have specific tax provisions for capital gains from Indian equities. While the STCG and LTCG rates for listed shares are generally the same, other rules like tax deducted at source (TDS) and reporting requirements might differ.

faq.q: Is Securities Transaction Tax (STT) applicable to IPO shares?
faq.a: Yes, STT is applicable on both the purchase and sale of listed equity shares, including IPO shares, transacted on a recognised stock exchange. The concessional tax rates for STCG and LTCG are contingent upon STT being paid.

faq.q: What if I don't sell my IPO shares?
faq.a: If you hold your IPO shares and do not sell them, there is no capital gain or loss realised, and thus no capital gains tax liability arises until you eventually sell them.

faq.q: Which ITR form should I use for IPO gains?
faq.a: If you have capital gains from IPOs and other income sources like salary or house property but no business income, ITR-2 is generally applicable. If you also have income from a business or profession, you would typically file ITR-3.
